videos.script: Draw Ana's sales table in the middle of a page. Put the date, the shop, the book and the promotion around it, and draw a line from each to the middle. {{star}} That is a star. Every question starts in the middle and is one step from any context it needs. {{one-step}} Now take the book and pull it apart. The category gets a table. The subcategory above it gets another. The department above that, a third. The publisher, a fourth. {{pull}} The star has grown arms, and the arms have branches. That is a snowflake. It is the same data, normalised again, inside the warehouse. {{snowflake}} Ana asks both the same question. Same answer, to the cent. One query joins three tables. The other joins six. {{same}} So why would anyone snowflake? Sometimes for good reasons, and this lesson names them. More often by habit, carried over from the operational database. {{why}} Then the pieces that make a star work across the whole warehouse. A dimension shared by two fact tables. One date table playing three roles. And the small flags that belong in a dimension of their own. {{pieces}}
